newsitem.title: UK: London's Docklands vision close to fruition.
newsitem.headline: London's Docklands vision close to fruition.

text.p: Sixteen years after Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government embarked on a partnership with the private sector to redevelop the run down Docklands area of east London, the vision has almost come to fruition.

Once the hub of London's international trade, only to degenerate into a barren wasteland in the 1960s, the Docklands have received over eight billion pounds ($13.5 billion) of investment, 75 percent of it from abroad.
Construction of the millennium exhibition centre is underway at nearby Greenwich, while the prominent Canary Wharf Tower stands out across London as evidence of the size of the project.
The development has not been trouble free.
At one stage, more than half of Canary Wharf tower's 50 floors stood unlet and there was even talk of the government moving an entire civil service department in to ensure the success of the venture.

An IRA bomb in 1996 also blew apart a section of the Docklands Light Railway (DLR) -- the main transportation route into the development -- and the buildings around it, causing millions of pounds worth of damage.
But the bomb did not deter investors.

"It actually had the reverse effect because the Docklands were projected all over the world," Sir Michael Pickard, chairman of London Docklands Development Corporation (LDDC), told a briefing on Monday of the quasi-governmental agency's annual report.
LDDC's remit runs out in March 1998 when its task will be complete.
The Canary Wharf tower is now 84 percent let and the business area thriving. Pickard attributed the success of the project to a strong partnership between the public and private sectors.
"It's a mixture of good pragmatism combined with running with a strong economy, and good entrepreneurialism," he said.

The latest vote of confidence in the Docklands has come from U.S. bank Citibank, a unit of Citicorp, which has begun constructing its new UK headquarters adjacent to Canary Wharf Tower. Designed by renowned architect Norman Foster, the new building will enhance the aesthetic appeal of the docks.
Citibank follows a long list of international companies already operating in Canary Wharf -- including BZW, AT&T and Courtaulds.
But critical to the successful functioning of the Docklands, as a business centre and expanding residential area, has been the construction of a reliable transport network.
The DLR has served been critical in this respect but the completion of the Jubilee line underground extension will boost the accessibility of the area -- and just in time for millennium.
The LDDC estimate the millennium exhibition centre will attract some 10 million tourists to the Docklands in 2000 compared with 1.6 million this year.

But that may not be the height of the Dockland's glory. The outgoing LDDC is hoping the construction of an international rowing course will boost London's chances of hosting the Olympic Games in either 2008 or 2012. ($ = 0.591 British Pounds)
